response.title: how to keep a refrigerator running during a power outage without a generator
response.answer:
You can keep a refrigerator running during a power outage without a gas generator by using a portable battery power station, a home backup battery, or a battery-and-inverter setup.

The best solution depends on how long you want the refrigerator to run: a few hours, overnight, or several days.

1. Best option: Portable battery power station

A portable power station is essentially a large rechargeable battery with standard AC outlets. You plug your refrigerator directly into it.

Unlike a gas generator, it:

Runs quietly, without exhaust fumes

Can be used safely indoors when operated according to its instructions

Requires no gasoline

Can be recharged from a wall outlet, solar panels, or sometimes a car

How long will a battery run your refrigerator?

A typical modern full-size refrigerator might use around 1–2 kWh of electricity per day, although actual consumption varies considerably.

Assuming 1.5 kWh/day and 85% battery-to-AC efficiency:

68 hours

These estimates assume normal cycling, not continuous compressor operation.

Important: A refrigerator's compressor can briefly draw several times its normal running power when starting. Look for a power station with enough AC output and surge capacity to start your particular refrigerator.

2. Some battery power stations worth considering

Good for refrigerators that need substantial compressor startup power.

Useful if you want to add battery capacity for longer outages.

3. Other ways to keep your refrigerator cold

Solar panels + battery: Add compatible solar panels to a portable power station. This can extend runtime during multiday outages, provided you get sufficient sunlight. Solar panels alone generally won't reliably run a normal refrigerator.

Home battery backup: A permanently installed system can automatically power selected household circuits during an outage. It's more expensive but convenient for frequent outages.

Ice or frozen water bottles: If you don't need the refrigerator compressor to run, use frozen ice packs or transfer food to an insulated cooler. According to the FDA, an unopened refrigerator keeps food cold for approximately four hours, while a full freezer can last around 48 hours. 
FDA
+1

Car battery + inverter: Technically possible, but a typical car starter battery is poorly suited to prolonged refrigerator operation. A properly fused deep-cycle battery and pure sine wave inverter are more appropriate. Never run a gasoline car in a garage to recharge it.

My recommendation: For a normal household refrigerator and an outage lasting around 24 hours, start by looking at a 2,000 Wh LiFePO₄ portable power station with at least 1,500–2,000 W of continuous AC output and adequate compressor-starting surge capacity.

One question: Are you trying to keep your refrigerator running for 12 hours, 24 hours, or 2–3 days? That will make a big difference in the battery size and cost.

You can keep a refrigerator running during a power outage **without a gas generator** by using a portable battery power station, a home backup battery, or a battery-and-inverter setup.

The best solution depends on how long you want the refrigerator to run: a few hours, overnight, or several days.

## 1. Best option: Portable battery power station

<AsyncImageGroup query={["EcoFlow DELTA 2 portable power station refrigerator plugged in","Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus portable power station home refrigerator backup","Anker SOLIX portable power station refrigerator backup"]} aspectRatio="5:4" shop_eligible={true}/>

A portable power station is essentially a large rechargeable battery with standard AC outlets. You plug your refrigerator directly into it.

Unlike a gas generator, it:
- Runs quietly, without exhaust fumes
- Can be used safely indoors when operated according to its instructions
- Requires no gasoline
- Can be recharged from a wall outlet, solar panels, or sometimes a car

### How long will a battery run your refrigerator?

A typical modern full-size refrigerator might use around 1–2 kWh of electricity per day, although actual consumption varies considerably.

Assuming 1.5 kWh/day and 85% battery-to-AC efficiency:

| Battery capacity | Estimated runtime |
|---|---|
| 500 Wh | 6–7 hours |
| 1,000 Wh | 13–14 hours |
| 2,000 Wh | 27 hours |
| 3,000 Wh | 41 hours |
| 5,000 Wh | 68 hours |

These estimates assume normal cycling, not continuous compressor operation.

**Important:** A refrigerator's compressor can briefly draw several times its normal running power when starting. Look for a power station with enough AC output and surge capacity to start your particular refrigerator.

## 2. Some battery power stations worth considering

## 3. Other ways to keep your refrigerator cold

**Solar panels + battery:** Add compatible solar panels to a portable power station. This can extend runtime during multiday outages, provided you get sufficient sunlight. Solar panels alone generally won't reliably run a normal refrigerator.

**Home battery backup:** A permanently installed system can automatically power selected household circuits during an outage. It's more expensive but convenient for frequent outages.

**Ice or frozen water bottles:** If you don't need the refrigerator compressor to run, use frozen ice packs or transfer food to an insulated cooler. According to the FDA, an unopened refrigerator keeps food cold for approximately four hours, while a full freezer can last around 48 hours. <Cite refs={["turn967641search1","turn967641search3"]}/>

**Car battery + inverter:** Technically possible, but a typical car starter battery is poorly suited to prolonged refrigerator operation. A properly fused deep-cycle battery and pure sine wave inverter are more appropriate. Never run a gasoline car in a garage to recharge it.

## 4. Calculate how much battery you need

{@body const [hours,setHours] = DIL.useState(24)}
{@body const capacity = Math.ceil((Number(daily)*1000*hours/24/0.85)/100)*100}

  </box>
  <box gap={2}>
    <row justify="between" align="center">

    </row>
    <slider min={6} max={72} step={6} value={hours} onChange={setHours}/>
    <row justify="between">
      <caption>6 hours</caption>
      <caption>72 hours</caption>
    </row>
  </box>
  <box background="surface-secondary" padding={3} radius="lg" gap={1}>
    <caption>Estimated minimum battery capacity</caption>
    <title size="2xl" color="default" tabularNums>{capacity.toLocaleString()} Wh</title>
    <text size="xs" color="secondary">Assumes 85% usable AC energy. Actual runtime varies with refrigerator cycling, battery reserve and inverter idle consumption.</text>
  </box>
</box>

**My recommendation:** For a normal household refrigerator and an outage lasting around 24 hours, start by looking at a 2,000 Wh LiFePO₄ portable power station with at least 1,500–2,000 W of continuous AC output and adequate compressor-starting surge capacity.

One question: **Are you trying to keep your refrigerator running for 12 hours, 24 hours, or 2–3 days?** That will make a big difference in the battery size and cost.
